record.paper_title: Open Problems in Understanding the Nuclear Chirality
record.original_question: What model-independent experimental fingerprints can identify chiral doublet bands in atomic nuclei unambiguously, especially in electromagnetic transitions, so that the diagnosis of chirality does not depend on subjective near-degeneracy criteria or on selection rules derived only from a specific rigid triaxial rotor plus one-particle-one-hole model?

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, a model independent selection rule for electromagnetic transitions in the chiral bands is still missing.
Again, new and model independent fingerprints are highly demanded.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In atomic nuclei, "nuclear chirality" refers to the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry that can occur in a triaxially deformed rotating nucleus when the total angular momentum vector lies outside any of the three principal planes of the triaxial shape, so that the angular momenta of the core, of valence protons, and of valence neutrons form either a left- or right-handed system. The standard signature of this phenomenon is the appearance of "chiral doublet bands": a pair of rotational bands with the same parity, similar spin assignments, and approximately degenerate energies, together with similar in-band B(M1) and B(E2) reduced electromagnetic transition probabilities.

Currently, identifying a pair of bands as a chiral doublet relies either on subjective criteria of near-degeneracy of energies and similarity of moments of inertia, or on selection rules for electromagnetic transitions derived from a specific microscopic model, namely the rigid triaxial rotor coupled to a single proton particle and a single neutron hole (one-particle–one-hole) configuration with frozen quasiparticle alignments.

Problem. Determine model-independent experimental fingerprints — formulated purely in terms of observable quantities (such as level energies, spin–parity assignments, and reduced electromagnetic transition probabilities B(M1), B(E2), B(E1), branching ratios, and possible staggering patterns thereof as functions of spin) — that:
(i) follow only from the underlying chiral geometry (i.e., from the existence of two energetically equivalent left- and right-handed angular-momentum configurations linked by an approximate chiral symmetry), without invoking any specific microscopic model of the intrinsic structure;
(ii) provide unambiguous selection rules and quantitative relations among electromagnetic transition matrix elements within and between the two partner bands, characterizing chirality in particular for configurations beyond the simple one-particle–one-hole-on-a-rigid-triaxial-rotor case (for example multi-quasiparticle or soft triaxial cores); and
(iii) allow one to discriminate experimentally between true chiral doublets and accidental near-degenerate band pairs that mimic chirality without possessing the underlying chiral geometry.

Provide and justify such a set of model-independent fingerprints, or prove that none exist beyond the criteria already known.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work has proposed several candidate model-independent or partially model-independent fingerprints — most prominently B(M1) staggering and B(M1)/B(E2) staggering as a function of spin, as well as selection rules associated with chirality–parity violation in nearly degenerate quartet bands. Reviews up to 2024 (e.g., the "25th anniversary of nuclear chirality" overview) still describe identification criteria for chiral doublets as not fully settled, and a universally accepted, completely model-independent set of electromagnetic fingerprints valid beyond the rigid triaxial rotor plus one-particle–one-hole picture has not been established. The problem is therefore best characterized as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Examining B(M1) staggering as a fingerprint for chiral doublet bands
status_evidence.snippet: Strong B(M1) staggering can be used as a fingerprint for static chirality in partner bands with near-degenerate energy spectra and similar B(M1) and B(E2) transitions.
status_evidence.claim: B(M1) staggering has been proposed as a fingerprint of nuclear chirality, partially addressing the question.

status_evidence.title: Selection rules of electromagnetic transitions for chirality-parity violation in atomic nuclei
status_evidence.snippet: Fingerprints for chirality-parity violation including nearly degenerate quartet bands and selection rules of electromagnetic transitions are provided.
status_evidence.claim: Additional selection rules for chirality (and chirality-parity) have been derived, indicating progress beyond the original 1p-1h triaxial rotor.

status_evidence.title: The 25th anniversary for nuclear chirality
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews status of identification criteria for chiral doublet bands in approximately 47 nuclei across A∼80, 100, 130, 190 mass regions.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2024, identification of chiral doublets continues to rely on a combination of criteria, with no single universally accepted fully model-independent fingerprint.
